## What we covered

Homework 1 first, then the start of module 2. The landscape of who delivers care,
physicians as the gatekeeper, what physician agency means, and the Dartmouth
figures on geographic variation, ending on why variation isn't the same thing as
waste. We ran the patient-side simulation at the end.

## Key points

- Medicine is learned by watching people work rather than from a rulebook, and
  there's real gray area in what care a patient needs. So variation in treatment
  across physicians is what you should expect. The question for this module is how
  much of it comes from something other than what the patient needs.
- Physician agency doesn't mean your doctor is trying to make money off you. The
  case that matters is the one where the care genuinely helps, just not by much,
  and costs more than you would have agreed to if anyone had told you the price.
  The test is whether you'd choose the same care if you had the physician's
  information and capabilities. The ear tube story is exactly that gap: a real
  but tiny benefit, a bill I didn't expect, and a decision I'd have made
  differently if I'd known what it would cost.
- The Dartmouth map is utilization, not prices. It's Medicare, which pays a
  formula adjusted for local wages, so adding up payments tells you how much care
  was delivered rather than what it cost. The figures are also adjusted for race,
  age, and sex, which is why "sicker people live there" doesn't account for the
  spread.
- Variation is not automatically waste. Waste is easy to name afterward and very
  hard to identify in advance, since you'd have to know which patients were going
  to get no benefit before treating them, and the work on predicting that finds it
  difficult. So the conclusion isn't that everyone should receive the same amount
  of care. It's that the sources of the variation are worth understanding, and
  payment incentives are the source we take up next.
- Not-for-profit status means one thing for certain, which is that revenue above
  costs doesn't go to owners. Tax treatment and access to capital follow from that.
  What's also supposed to follow, community benefit, isn't well measured or well
  regulated, so a not-for-profit can end up looking a lot like a for-profit in how
  it behaves. A C-suite person I worked with in a health system put it as no
  mission without margin.

## Thursday

Model day, and the place in this module where the math gets in the way if you
haven't seen the notation once already. Read the slides and the chapter before you
come. The pieces: $x$ is the amount of care, $B(x)$ is the benefit of that care to
the patient, $P$ is the price the patient pays, and net benefit is the benefit
minus what you pay for it. We'll maximize those functions, so be comfortable with
derivatives, and we'll do a constrained maximization in a simplified way by
substituting one thing into another rather than setting up a Lagrangian. The
physician maximizes something by choosing an amount of care, the patient maximizes
something by choosing an amount of care, and we compare the two under different
ways of paying for care.

Next week is a quiz on Tuesday and a panel on Thursday, then fall break.

## Homework

Grades and comments for homework 1 are in Canvas, so read your comment. Email me
if something looks wrong, since we could have missed something in reviewing your
repositories. An answer key is coming.

Three things to carry into homework 2. Merge on identifiers, not names, because
county names repeat across states and merging on the name duplicates rows until
you have far more data than you started with. A national rate isn't the average of
the county rates, so weight by counts or sum the numerator and the denominator
before dividing. And use git the way it's meant to be used, working locally,
committing, then pushing. Uploading files through the GitHub website cost nobody
points this time and will cost points next time.
